name: Priya Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Priya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions or parties. What you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work chat for an online furniture shop, mostly the escalations, so sofas that arrived ripped or wardrobes missing half the screws. I run three or four chats at once, with an AI assistant drafting replies that I fix before sending. I love the detective part, working out from a blurry photo whether it was the courier or the factory. What wears me out is the same refund argument twenty times a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm twenty-seven and I live on my own in a one-bed flat I bought last year, with help from my grandmother's inheritance. I've got about seven months of pay saved on top of that. Weekends I do pottery classes and see my sister, who's a nurse. I'm pretty sensible with money, but I'll take a punt on a new idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. The drafting tool we use still writes things like we apologise for the inconvenience to someone whose sofa is in pieces. It's fine for the easy stuff, and that's where it stops. I'd probably post a funny screenshot of that in a group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays, and the boring half gets a bit lighter. I'd still be the one deciding whether we refund or send a courier. Honestly that's a good outcome for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the drafting tool every day and build my own saved prompts for the common cases, like damaged legs or wrong colour. I'd ask my manager about the quality analyst role, the person who reviews chats. And I'd keep paying extra off the mortgage, about two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by the idea, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bored. Would that be a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I like new things, and a world where AI fizzles out feels flat. I'd probably start messing about with something on the side, like an online pottery shop, just to have a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else weighing on you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, which I know is lucky. The flat's mine, the mortgage is small, and there's always another chat job if this shop closes.

I'd share a **funny screenshot** of a bad AI apology in a group chat.

Ask about the **quality analyst** role that reviews chats.
Keep paying an extra **£200 a month** off the mortgage.
feel: **Calm**, with a little boredom at nothing new happening.

fieldNote: Priya already **uses AI daily** and sees its limits up close.

She'd start a **side project** partly out of boredom, not need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learn the tools will be fine and the people who refuse will struggle. I'd say it kindly, though, because some of my team are scared. Online I might write a short post about how I use AI on chats, to show it's not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the furniture shop would cut the chat team by half within two years. The simple chats, like where's my order, go first. I'd want to be in the half that stays, the one doing the tricky judgment calls and checking the bot's answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to help set up the new chatbot, testing it on real cases, in the first month. I'd do an online course on data basics, like reading dashboards, maybe three hours a week. And I'd ask for a pay rise once I'm the one who knows the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. I'd feel like there's a race on and I'm near the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said near the front. What if you're wrong about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have the flat and seven months saved, and lots of call centres nearby. I'd lose a job, not my home. That's a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise, who's been there twelve years and still prints her rota. She's lovely with customers and terrified of anything new. I'd probably try to sit with her and show her the tools.

I might write a short post showing AI **isn't magic** on chats.

Take an online **data basics** course for three hours a week.
Ask for a **pay rise** once I know the system best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to take it seriously, not to panic. I'd probably be the one at work explaining what AGI means to people over lunch. I'd also say we need some kind of safety net, because two years is brutal for lots of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, my job is gone, full stop. There's nothing in chat support an AGI can't do, including the detective bit with the blurry photos. Even the person checking the bot probably goes within a year after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to get into something where people still want a human, or where there are hands. I'd look at the warehouse side, managing the returns and repairs team, since robots come three years later. I'd also put a chunk of savings into an index fund, because the companies doing this will make money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but I'd be thinking about it every night for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job's gone, full stop. Why anxious and not more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I own the flat, I've got savings, and I'm good at picking things up. Plenty of people will be in a much worse spot. I'd be scared, but I'd have options to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots, three years later, for the warehouse side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have had three years managing people and a repairs workshop, which is more than I have now. After that, I honestly don't know. Nobody does.

say: I'd say **take it seriously**, not panic, and explain AGI over lunch.
I'd also argue for a **safety net**, because two years is brutal.
think: My **chat job** is gone, including the detective work with photos.

do: Move to managing the **returns and repairs** team on the warehouse side.
Put a chunk of savings into an **index fund**.
Use the two years to find work with **hands or people**.
feel: **Anxious**, thinking about it every night for a while.
S2.quote: There's nothing in chat support an AGI can't do, including the detective bit with the blurry photos.
fieldNote: Even an **adaptive** worker sees no safe corner in chat work under fast AGI.
Owning the flat and savings keep her **anxious, not alarmed**.
She uses the **three-year robot gap** to shift towards the warehouse.

steps.text: Apply to manage the warehouse returns and repairs team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window and companies should be retraining people now. At work I'd push for the shop to tell us its plans early. I'd probably post that somewhere too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd actually come out of it well. Five years is long enough to become the person who runs the AI side of customer service, and then move on before that goes too. I'd be thirty-two with a good CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get myself onto the team that runs the chatbot. Then I'd do a part-time course in operations management, maybe two years at evening classes. I'd keep investing and keep the pottery shop going as a small earner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a lot more hopeful than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move on before that goes too. Move on to what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running the warehouse or the repairs workshop, or something with physical stuff. AI does the thinking first, so I want to end up near things with hands for a while. After that I'd see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I might rent out the spare corner of the flat on weekends if things got tight. But I'd not plan a big move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and nobody should waste it. I'd probably write a long post about it, which my sister would tease me for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'd have a whole career change's worth of time. I think I'd do well out of it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the chat job for two or three years and learn everything about the AI tools. Then I'd move into operations or start my own small business, maybe a furniture repair service, because I already know what breaks. I'd keep saving and investing steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A furniture repair service is quite a jump from chat. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've spent five years looking at photos of broken sofas. I know which legs snap and which fabric rips. Ten years is long enough to learn upholstery and build up customers before robots get good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock that plan off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me getting comfortable. If the job's easy and pays well, I might coast. I'd have to set myself a deadline.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only one where being quick isn't enough. What would help is employers paying for real retraining in the time before it hits, and some kind of income support for people while they switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the customers would feel. People already hate talking to bots about a broken sofa. The first shops to keep a human on the line might win customers for a while.

headlineQuote: People already hate talking to bots about a broken sofa. The first shops to keep a human on the line might win customers for a while.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** chat agent handling escalations for an online furniture shop.
She **owns her flat**, has seven months saved, and uses AI tools every day.
She stays calm or uneasy except under **fast AGI**, where she becomes anxious.
Her plans move from chatbot operations towards **hands-on work** like furniture repair.
She worries more for **colleagues** who fear new tools than for herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being quick isn't enough.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** for people while they switch jobs.
